# Quality Report

`mxcli report` with no kind is the **scored** report: it runs every lint rule, groups
the findings into categories (Security, Quality, Architecture, Performance, Naming,
Design, and Other for unmapped rules), scores each, and weighs them into one number
out of 100. The other reports each answer one question
(`report-architecture`, `report-security`, `report-tests`, `report-performance`,
`report-traceability`, `report-map`); this one is the summary across all rules.

## Run it

```bash
mxcli report -p app.mpr -o docs/quality.md
mxcli report -p app.mpr --format html -o docs/quality.html
mxcli report -p app.mpr --format json -o docs/quality.json   # for CI, or to compare runs
# the app's own modules only, without Marketplace and platform modules
mxcli report -p app.mpr --modules Sales,Billing
```

It builds a full catalog first, so the first run on a project takes a while.

## Before trusting the number

- **Are all the rules running?** Without a `.claude/lint-rules/` directory beside the
  project (or above it, up to the repository root), only the built-in rules run and the
  bundled Starlark rules do not. The report warns on stderr, and the score looks
  *better*, because fewer rules can find anything. `mxcli init` installs them.
  `mxcli lint -p app.mpr --list-rules` shows what runs.
- **Which modules?** Without `--modules`, Marketplace and platform modules count too,
  and their findings are not yours to fix. With `--modules`, project-wide findings —
  security level, demo users, user-role mappings — are left out (they are about no
  one module). Use both: the full run for the project's settings, the scoped run
  for the code the team owns.
- **Does it build?** The score does not include Mendix's own consistency check.
  A project with CE errors can score well. Run `mxcli docker check -p app.mpr` as
  well (ako/mxcli#2423 tracks putting it in the report).

## Reading the score

Each category starts at 100 and loses a fixed amount **per finding** (an error costs
far more than a warning, a warning more than an info), floored at 0. The overall
score is a weighted average with Security weighted highest. The amounts and weights
live in `mdl/linter/report.go`.

Two consequences:

- **The penalty does not scale with the app.** A large app with many intended
  findings of one rule — row-level access rules, say — can sit at 0 in a category for
  reasons that are all deliberate. Read the findings, not the number.
- **The number is for comparison, not for judgement.** Record it at a known point
  (the template's first build, a release) and compare later runs with it; a score
  that fell is a finding. `bootstrap-app` records this baseline.

The **Detailed Findings** table is what to work through: the rule, its severity, where,
and why. `mxcli lint -p app.mpr` gives the same findings for one module or one
document (`--modules`, `--documents`) while fixing them.

## Accepting a finding

When a finding is intended, record that decision once, in the project brain, rather
than ignoring it:

```bash
mxcli brain capture "Beperking has no access rules on purpose" \
  --accepts "SEC001:read only through DS_Beperkingen_Inzien, which logs every view" \
  -a @Dossier.Beperking -p app.mpr
```

The report then counts it apart ("Accepted (brain decisions, not scored)") and does not
score it; `lint` leaves it out of the open findings, and `report security` shows the
rule as accepted. A decision with no anchor accepts a project-wide finding (SEC013,
SEC003). When the rule stops firing there, `mxcli lint` reports the acceptance as
stale. `mxcli lint --show-accepted` lists what is accepted, with the deciding entry.

Accept only what is decided. Code still being written belongs in a lint baseline
(`mxcli lint --baseline lint-baseline.json --update-baseline`), which tracks new
findings without saying anything is intended.
